title: Ticket Booking
subtitle: High-concurrency ticket reservations: virtual waiting rooms, two-phase temporary seat holds, and optimistic concurrency.
keyTakeaways: Prevent double-booking using a two-phase seat reservation pattern: Phase 1 acquires an atomic 10-minute temporary hold (AVAILABLE -> HELD) using Redis Lua or DB optimistic concurrency, and Phase 2 transitions HELD -> BOOKED upon payment confirmation.

Protect the core booking database during major concert drops (millions of concurrent users competing for 50,000 seats) using an Edge Virtual Waiting Room (Queue-it token-bucket model) that admits users to checkout at a controlled, sustainable rate.

Never rely solely on Redis key expiration events to release abandoned holds: store hold_expires_at directly in the database seat row so any query or compare-and-swap update treats an expired hold as immediately available.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A Ticket Booking System allows customers to browse event venues, select specific numbered seats, temporarily reserve them during checkout, and purchase tickets without the risk of double-booking.
bullets: Functional: View interactive venue seat maps with live seat availability; reserve seats on temporary 10-minute hold; purchase held seats via payment gateways; release abandoned holds automatically.
Functional: Search events by artist, venue, and date.
Non-Functional: Strict zero double-booking guarantee under any concurrency condition.
Non-Functional: Extreme flash-sale resilience: withstand millions of fans hitting the seat selection page simultaneously during major stadium tours.
Out of Scope: Secondary ticket resale market auctions, physical wristband NFC scanning at gates, and dynamic ticket pricing algorithms.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Ticket booking systems experience extreme load spikes: normal days have minimal traffic, while stadium concert drops create catastrophic traffic surges.
bullets: Flash Sale Peak: 5 million fans arrive within 60 seconds for a 50,000-seat stadium show (~80,000 requests/second at peak).
Inventory Constraints: A single stadium contains exactly 50,000 seats. All 50,000 seats sell out within 3 to 5 minutes.
Payment Funnel: Average checkout takes 4 to 8 minutes (filling billing details, completing 3D Secure bank OTP).
Concurrency Hotspot: Multiple users clicking the exact same front-row seat simultaneously creates intense database row lock contention.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Calculations demonstrate why raw database queries cannot survive an unmitigated concert ticket drop without a rate-limiting admission queue.
bullets: Database bottleneck: A relational database handles 2,000 to 5,000 writes/second. If 100,000 users attempt to hold the same block of seats simultaneously, database connection pools exhaust and crash within seconds.

Queue admission sizing: If 50,000 seats are available and each user buys 2 tickets on average, only 25,000 successful transactions are possible. Admitting 200 users/second into the seat map drains the queue smoothly across 2 to 3 minutes without stressing the database.
Memory footprint: 50,000 seats * 64 bytes per seat state in Redis = ~3.2 MB of RAM per event, meaning an entire season of concerts fits in a modest Redis instance.

codeSnippet.title: Ticket Booking Capacity & Flash-Sale Sizing Worksheet
codeSnippet.code:
================================================================================
TICKET BOOKING CAPACITY WORKSHEET (3M TICKETS/DAY + 5M USER FLASH SALE)
================================================================================
1. THROUGHPUT (BASELINE vs. STADIUM FLASH SALE)
   - Avg Seat-Map Read QPS    : 500,000,000 / 86,400        = 5,787 QPS
   - Flash-Sale Read QPS      : 5M users / 10s refresh      = 500,000 QPS
   - Avg Booking Write QPS    : 3,000,000 * 2 / 86,400      = 69 QPS
   - Flash-Sale Hold Write QPS: Throttled by Waiting Room   = 10,000 QPS

2. REDIS MEMORY (100% OF ACTIVE SEAT INVENTORY IN RAM)
   - Active Shows (100K)      : 100,000 shows * 2,000 seats = 200,000,000 seats
   - Per-Seat Cache Entry     : 64 bytes                    = 12.8 GB
   - Waiting Room ZSETs (10M) : 10,000,000 users * 64 bytes = 640 MB
   - Total Redis Cluster (2x) : ~13.5 GB * 2 (Replica)      = 27.0 GB RAM

3. 5-YEAR ACID DATABASE STORAGE
   - Daily Show Seat Rows     : 200M seats * 128 B          = 25.6 GB / day
   - Daily Booking Orders     : 3M orders * 1 KB            = 3.0 GB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Storage       : 28.6 GB * 365 * 5           = 52.2 TB
   - 3x Replicated + Indexes  : 52.2 TB * 3 * 1.3           = 203.6 TB

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH (STADIUM SEAT MAP = 80,000 SEATS)
   - Compact Seat Bitmap Size : 80,000 seats * 2 bits       = 20 KB
   - Peak Egress (500K QPS)   : 500,000 * 20 KB             = 10.0 GB/s (80 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: APIs separate queue admission tokens from seat holds and final booking transactions.
bullets: Waiting Room Token: `POST /v1/queue/enter` returns `{ queueToken, estimatedWaitSeconds, position }`.
Hold Seats API: `POST /v1/events/{eventId}/seats/hold` takes `{ seatIds: [101, 102], queueToken }` and returns `{ holdId, expiresAt: 1727789400 }`.
Confirm Booking API: `POST /v1/bookings/confirm` takes `{ holdId, paymentToken }` and returns `{ bookingId, status: "CONFIRMED" }`.
Seats Table: `seats` (`seat_id`, `event_id`, `section`, `row`, `number`, `status: AVAILABLE|HELD|BOOKED`, `held_by_user_id`, `hold_expires_at`, `version`).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture uses an edge virtual waiting room to throttle traffic before it reaches the core seat reservation engine.
bullets: Virtual Waiting Room (Edge CDN / Queue-it): Holds excess fans in an off-origin queue, issuing signed HMAC admission cookies at a controlled rate (e.g., 200 users/second).
Seat Inventory Service (Redis): Tracks live seat availability (`AVAILABLE`, `HELD`, `BOOKED`) and executes atomic hold operations via Lua scripts.
Booking Relational DB (PostgreSQL): Authoritative source of record using Optimistic Concurrency Control (`version` column) for final booking state.
Payment Gateway Adapter: Communicates with payment processors outside database transactions.
Hold Expiration Janitor: Background worker releasing expired holds, complemented by lazy expiration checks during customer read queries.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: The two-phase reservation pattern guarantees that seats are held exclusively during checkout without locking database tables indefinitely.
bullets: Phase 1: Temporary Hold (10-minute hold): The user selects seat #101. An atomic Redis Lua script checks if the seat is `AVAILABLE`. If yes, it transitions state to `HELD`, records the user ID, sets an expiration timestamp (now + 600s), and returns success. If another user attempts to hold the same seat 2ms later, the script returns an error.

Phase 2: Payment and Confirmation: The user completes credit card payment. The server executes a database update: `UPDATE seats SET status = "BOOKED" WHERE seat_id = 101 AND status = "HELD" AND hold_expires_at > NOW()`. If the hold has expired, the update affects 0 rows, triggering an automatic payment refund.

Lazy expiration on query: When any user queries a seat map, the query evaluates `IF (status == "HELD" AND hold_expires_at < NOW()) THEN status = "AVAILABLE"`. This eliminates race conditions where Redis key expiration events might be delayed.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Hardening flash-sale platforms requires preventing bot scrapers, handling payment timeouts, and ensuring fair queue distribution.
bullets: Cryptographically signed queue cookies: The Virtual Waiting Room signs admission tokens using HMAC-SHA256 with a 15-minute expiration. The API Gateway validates the signature before allowing any request to reach the hold service, preventing users from bypassing the queue.

Mitigating inventory hoarding: Limit each user to a maximum of 4 or 6 seats per transaction, and restrict each user to one active hold at a time to prevent scalpers from locking large blocks of seats.

Payment gateway callback timeouts: If payment confirmation takes longer than the 10-minute hold window, check the payment status with the gateway before releasing the seat. If the card was charged, honor the booking.

tradeOffs.pros: Protects backend databases from crashing under 5M-user flash surges; provides a fair, transparent user experience.
tradeOffs.cons: Adds architectural complexity and requires CDN edge coordination or external vendor integration (Queue-it).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Major concert ticket drops, high-demand sporting events, and viral limited-edition product drops.

tradeOffs.pros: Simpler architecture; no waiting screens for users during normal low-traffic events.
tradeOffs.cons: Databases experience massive lock contention and connection pool exhaustion under sudden traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Local community theaters, regular cinema screenings, and low-concurrency reservation systems.

tradeOffs.option: Redis Lua Hold with Lazy Database Expiration
tradeOffs.pros: Sub-millisecond seat selection response times; resilient against Redis expiration event delivery delays.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires maintaining state synchronization between Redis cache and relational database records.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput reserved-seating systems with interactive graphical seat maps.

interviewTip: When designing a ticket booking platform, focus on two key areas: first, propose an Edge Virtual Waiting Room to throttle 5 million concurrent fans down to 200 users/second; second, explain the two-phase hold pattern (temporary 10-minute hold followed by final payment confirmation) with lazy expiration to prevent double-booking.
